DJI Dock 4 + Matrice 5TDBattery swap

Built in Blender from DJI's spec page, manuals and launch footage, with the dock checked to the millimetre against both published envelopes. Play a full turnaround: landing, cover closing, the 25-second battery swap, cover opening and take-off. Switch to X-ray or Cut-away to watch the battery leave the tail, ride the rotor to a compartment and come back charged.

Transfer ring seen from behind, live

Lead screw
0 / 185 mm

The aircraft's battery bay and the four compartments lie on one circle (radius 165 mm, estimated) around a rotor axis parallel to the aircraft. The cradle turns with the rotor; its hook rides a lead screw along that axis to pull or push a battery. The hatch plate opposite the cradle closes the pad when the rotor is home.

Batteries 4 packs, 3 stored at most

IDWhereLevelState

One compartment always stays free so the rotor can put the used battery down before it fetches a charged one. Two packs charge at a time (27 min, 15 → 95 %). Levels in the clip are set at the start; the LED patterns follow user manual p. 71.

Swap sequence select to jump

    DJI states under 25 s from cover fully closed to swap complete, and under 45 s from landing to take-off. DJI publishes no sub-step timing; the split here is an estimate that adds up to 25.0 s.

    What the model is based on

    • DJIClosed 639 × 640 × 836 mm, open 1750 × 640 × 550 mm, 4 compartments holding at most 3 batteries, 2 charging channels, swap under 25 s, battery 172.9 × 96.02 × 67.7 mm. The battery leaves through the tail; the aircraft stays powered by the pad's wireless coil.
    • DJIPart numbering: dock items 1–14 (user manual p. 24), aircraft items (p. 10), battery LED bands (p. 71), footprint 567 × 555 mm on a 400 × 400 mm bolt pattern (installation manual p. 44).
    • FittedThe aircraft. DJI's Matrice 5TD STEP is cut off on DJI's server before any face was written, but its 95,153 vertex points survive in assembly coordinates. Fuselage sections, motor centres, battery bay, gimbal and LiDAR are fitted to them.
    • FittedSwap layout: a rotor on an axis parallel to the aircraft, a C-shaped cage with compartments at about 10:30, 9, 7 and 5 o'clock seen from behind, a cradle with a lead screw and hook. Read from DJI's launch film (62–77 s), Drone DR1's render and KOSECO's footage of the cradle rising behind the H marker.
    • EstimateTransfer radius 165 mm, rotor axis 320 mm above the ground, hook stroke 185 mm, screw pitch 8 mm, hinge positions, hump profile of the pad, the hatch plate opposite the cradle, and the split of the 25 s into 15 steps.

    01 · Scenarios

    Operating scenarios for Dock 4

    DJI names six uses for Dock 4: first response, infrastructure inspection, overnight security, surveying, rescue and remote sites. In each one, the battery swap replaces a recharge between flights. The bars show airborne minutes per hour for a typical flight in each scenario, computed from DJI's charge and flight times (method in section 02).

    02 · Generations

    Dock 2, Dock 3 and Dock 4 compared

    Figures from DJI's spec sheets for each dock and its aircraft. The biggest change is what happens between flights: Dock 2 and Dock 3 recharge their one battery inside the aircraft, while Dock 4 replaces it with a charged one. The hour view below shows what that does to flying time.

    One hour at the dockRecharge the battery in the aircraft, or swap it for a charged one

    20 min
    • Flying
    • On the pad: battery charging in the aircraft
    • On the pad: battery swap, landing to take-off under 45 s
    • Lower strip: charge of the battery in the aircraft, 0 to 100 %
    1. Dock 2 and Dock 3 have one battery. It stays in the aircraft. After every flight the aircraft waits on the pad while the dock recharges it: 27 min from 15 to 95 % on Dock 3, 32 min from 20 to 90 % on Dock 2.
    2. Dock 4 has four batteries. One is in the aircraft and three wait in compartments. After landing, the dock pulls the used battery out of the tail and pushes a charged one in. The swap takes under 25 s; landing to take-off, under 45 s.
    3. The used battery charges while the aircraft flies. Two charging channels each take a battery from 15 to 95 % in 27 min. In this model a charged battery is ready at every landing, at every flight length on the slider.

    How the strips are worked out: a flight drains the battery at the hover rate (100 % divided by the maximum hover time, per minute). Dock 2 and Dock 3 put that charge back at DJI's published charging speed, plus 20 s for landing and closing the cover. Dock 4 spends 45 s on the pad per landing. Each strip is one hour from a long day of back-to-back flights, picked so that its flying time equals the day's average. Wind, cold and payload shorten real flights.

    03 · Sample data

    One day at a Dock 4 site, sample data

    A simulated 24 hours at one dock: night patrols, emergency dispatches and two inspection flights, with a wind front in the afternoon. The batteries, swaps, holds and charging follow the dock's published limits. Every value on these screens is generated for this page; it is not a recording and not DJI software.

    SIMULATED

    The screens are a generic layout made for this page. Behaviour follows DJI's published rules where they exist: no take-off above 12 m/s wind, a swap only when the aircraft is below 90 % and a stored battery is above 90 %, two batteries charging at 27 min from 15 to 95 %, at most three batteries in the compartments. Consumption, flight lengths, the weather and the scene in the camera view are invented.

    Sources: DJI Dock 4 specs · DJI Dock 4 announcement · DJI Dock 3 specs · DJI Dock 2 specs · DJI Dock 4 User Manual v1.0 (swap rule p. 70, battery LEDs p. 71).
